div.p: From a fresh install to a published vCard in under five minutes. Five decisions, one publish click.

div.h2: 01Pick a slug you'll be proud to print
div.p: Your slug is the part of the URL after your domain — yoursite.com/your-name. It shows up in QR scans, NFC taps, and email signatures, so make it readable and memorable. Lowercase, hyphenated, ideally your name or initials.
You can change it later, but old links break — nobody you've already given a card to will get redirected. Pick once, well.
div.div: Slugs are checked for uniqueness as you type. If jane-doe is taken, the form suggests jane-doe-2. We recommend something more distinct, like adding a middle initial or your company.
div.p: Three image inputs do most of the visual work:

ol.li: Profile photo. Square, at least 400×400px. Faces convert dramatically better than logos for individual cards — use a real headshot.
Banner image. Wide aspect (3:1 or wider), 1200px+ across. This is the band behind your name. A muted brand background tends to outperform busy stock photography.
QR logo overlay. Optional. A small mark inside your QR code; useful when the QR is printed alongside other brands.

div.p: The two color pickers — primary and secondary — drive every accent on your card. Primary is the page background; secondary is the action color (buttons, links, highlights). Pick a high-contrast pair.

img.alt: The profile-photo, banner, and color-picker section of the /get-started form

figure.figcaption: Fig. 1Branding inputs on the card setup form — profile, banner, primary + secondary color.

div.p: You can fill every field, but you don't need to. The fields that get used:

ul.li: Name, role, company. Always shown.
Mobile. Tap-to-call works on phones — most card scans happen on phones.
Email. Tap-to-mail.
One website. Your company URL. Not five.
One or two social links. LinkedIn for B2B, Instagram for B2C, Calendly if you want bookings. Pick the two people will actually click.

div.p: Resist the temptation to add every social network you've ever joined. A card with two clear actions converts better than a card with twelve.
ships with five layout templates. They differ in how prominent the photo, banner, and lead form are — not in what data they show. Switch templates anytime; your data is preserved.

ul.li: Modern (default) — balanced layout with banner, profile photo, and prominent lead CTA. The safe pick if you're unsure.
Classic — photo-forward, traditional vCard feel. Best for people-first cards (consultants, agents, founders).
Minimal — pared down to name, role, and contact methods. For cards going on densely-printed materials where the QR carries most of the design.
Corporate — banner-led, company-forward. Best for cards where the brand outweighs the individual.
Creative — color-led, photography-heavy. For brands with strong visual identity (designers, agencies, hospitality).

img.alt: The five template thumbnails from the /get-started template picker

figure.figcaption: Fig. 2The five templates shipped with , shown in the picker.

div.p: The right side of the form shows a live preview as you type. When you're happy, hit Submit. creates a real Odoo website.page at your slug — visit it directly, share the URL, or download your QR.

From your card's form view in the backend, the Publish / Unpublish smart button toggles whether the page is live. Backend edits to any visible field auto-regenerate the published page — you don't need to click "Generate" again.
Next: how to actually distribute your card so the work pays off.
Four channels — QR, NFC, URL, email signature. Each has a job. Use the right one for the moment.
From your card's backend form view, click Download QR Code. You get a high-resolution PNG you can drop on:

ul.li: Printed business cards (the original use case)
Conference badges and lanyards
Trade-show booth backdrops
Slide deck title pages and last-slide CTAs
Restaurant tabletops, retail signage, vehicle wraps

div.p: Print it big enough that someone two meters away can scan it. As a rule of thumb, the QR should be at least 1/10th the distance between the QR and the eye of the person scanning it.
div.div: The QR includes a small brand logo overlay by default. You can swap it for your own brand mark in the card's settings — see Setting Up Your Card.
div.p: NFC cards are the upgrade over QR for face-to-face. The other person taps your card to their phone, your URL opens — no camera, no app, no QR-scanning friction.
The full programming walkthrough lives in the NFC Card Programming guide. The short version: buy a writable NTAG215 card, install NFC Tools on your phone, write your card's URL, done.
Your card has a normal web URL. Use it everywhere a link goes:

ul.li: SMS / WhatsApp: "Here's my card: yoursite.com/jane-doe"
LinkedIn "Featured" section — pin it as a featured link
Instagram / TikTok bio — replace your linktree
Calendly intake page — link your card from "About me"
Slack / Notion profile — for distributed teams

div.p: includes an email signature generator. From the backend, open your user record and use the signature builder to produce HTML you can paste into your email client's signature settings — the same flow whether you use Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, or anything else.
Email signatures are the most-used and most-undervalued distribution channel. Every email you send is a card share. Set this up once and forget it.

div.h1: Turn card visits into qualified leads.
div.p: Five settings stand between an anonymous scan and a CRM-ready opportunity. This is how to configure them.

By default, your card is read-only — visitors see your contact info, that's it. To capture leads, toggle Show form on. A "Get In Touch" button appears on your card; tapping it opens a modal with the lead form.
You can rename the button to match your goal — Book a meeting, Get my pricing PDF, Join the waitlist. The button label sets the user's expectation; match what happens after submission.
Lead tags travel with each captured lead into your CRM, where they become filterable, sortable, and reportable. Use them as your top-level segmentation:

ul.li: Source tags — conference-q2, print-card, linkedin-bio
Intent tags — demo-requested, info-only, partner-inquiry
Owner tags — jane-territory, enterprise-team

div.p: Tags applied at capture time are far more reliable than tags applied later, when context is lost.

Every lead captured gets added to a mailing list automatically. Pick a focused list rather than your master "Newsletter" — the more specific the list, the more permission you have to send specific follow-up.
If the list doesn't exist yet, type its name into the field; creates it on the fly when the first lead lands.
div.div: Visitors don't see the mailing list name, but they do see (per Odoo's mass mailing rules) a footer when they receive emails. Pick a name you'd be comfortable showing.
div.h2: 04Write the CTA and thank-you that convert
div.p: Two short copy fields — under-tuned by most users, high-leverage when you do.

ol.li: Lead button label: verb + outcome. "Get my pricing" beats "Submit". "See a demo" beats "Contact us".

Thank-you message: appears after submission. Set expectations: "Thanks. Jane will email you within one business day with your industry benchmarks." A specific promise outperforms "Thanks for reaching out!"

div.h2: 05Tag leads to a trade show or event
div.p: The Active Event picker (in the Lead Collection Form Settings group, just below Tags) lets you stamp every lead captured by your card with a specific event. The use case is in-person work — you're at a booth, an open house, a golf outing, a conference. Set it to the event you're staffing today, and every scan that lands while it's set carries that event with it forever.

ul.li: The picker only shows events that haven't ended yet, so you can't accidentally pick last year's show.
Each captured lead's CRM form will show a small Captured at: <event> badge under the title — visible to you and to anyone reviewing the lead later.
Standard CRM filters — saved searches like "leads from SaaStr 2026" — work out of the box once event_id is set.

div.div: Remember to clear the picker after the show ends. Otherwise the next walk-in scan that lands on your card next week will still be tagged with last week's event. (We may add a daily cron later that auto-clears it the day after the event ends — for now it's manual.)
div.h2: 06Where leads end up in your CRM
div.p: Each form submission creates a crm.lead opportunity in the default pipeline stage. The lead has:

ul.li: Contact name, email, phone — captured directly from the form
The originating partner.vcard linked back, so you can see "this lead came from Jane's card"
Any tags you configured at capture time
Free-text notes if the form's notes field is enabled

div.p: Leads land in your CRM's default pipeline stage (the first stage in your pipeline — typically "New") and get auto-assigned to the card's owner: looks up the user whose login matches the card's email, and falls back to the user who created the card record. For team-level routing rules beyond that, see the admin guide: CRM & Lead Routing.

img.alt: The Submission Tracking tab on a captured lead's form view

figure.figcaption: Fig. 3A captured lead's Submission Tracking tab — IP, location, device, browser, OS.

div.p: Reviews on your card become a structured asset in your database — moderate, surface, and reuse them across your stack.
From the backend form view, toggle Show reviews on. A reviews block appears on your card with a "Leave a review" call-to-action and any approved reviews so far.
Visitors leave reviews via a modal: name, rating (1–5), and a free-text comment. The modal is the same one used for the lead form, so tone-of-voice stays consistent.

New reviews don't appear publicly until you approve them — every submission lands with is_published = false by default. From the backend, the Reviews menu shows pending submissions with reviewer name, rating, comment, and timestamp. Toggle Published to approve, or delete the row to reject.
A handful of approved reviews is more credible than a wall of them. Five strong reviews beat fifty mediocre ones.
Approved reviews show up in three places:

ul.li: On your published card — in the reviews block, ordered most-recent-first.
In Odoo backend — under the Reviews menu, filterable by rating and card.
In your weekly digest email — see Email Automations & Digests.

div.p: For org-wide review reporting (e.g., average rating across your team), see the admin track's CRM & Lead Routing guide.
